summary: Defines the ENABLE command for IMAP. Most IMAP extensions can simply be used if the server supports them, but a few change server behavior and so need the client to opt in. ENABLE lets a client tell the server which of those extensions it understands. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Before a waiter brings a special menu, the guest says they can read it. ENABLE lets an email program tell the server which extra features it understands.

subtitle: How an IMAP client tells the server which opt-in extensions it understands.

tldr.problem: Some IMAP extensions make the server send extra unsolicited responses, but the server cannot send them until it knows the client will not choke on them.
tldr.mechanism: The ENABLE command lets the client list the extensions it wants, and the server answers with an untagged ENABLED response naming the ones it turned on.
tldr.outcome: Clients get one explicit way to opt in. At publication, CONDSTORE was the only extension that needed it, and the RFC discourages designing new extensions that require ENABLE.

facts.label: Valid in state
facts.value: Authenticated, before any mailbox is selected

today: RFC 5161 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text names CONDSTORE as the only extension that needed ENABLE at the time of publication.

sections.title: Why Clients Need to Opt In
sections.content:
Several IMAP extensions let the server return unsolicited responses specific to the extension. A server cannot send those until it knows the client supports the extension and will not choke on the extra data.

Until now, extensions usually said that the server may not send such responses until the client has used a command carrying extension data. CONDSTORE does this with a SELECT or FETCH parameter, and ANNOTATE uses a side effect of FETCH. Each extension invented its own signal.

RFC 5161 replaces that patchwork with one explicit signal: a new ENABLE command. Most IMAP extensions do not require the client to enable them in any way.
sections.eli5: Some features make the server say extra things. The server wants to be sure you can understand them first, so now there is one clear way to say yes.

sections.title: The ENABLE Command
sections.content:
ENABLE takes a list of capability names. It returns OK when the relevant capabilities are enabled and BAD when there are no arguments or an argument has a syntax error. Once enabled, an extension stays active until the IMAP connection is closed, and there is no way to disable it.

For each argument the server does one of three things:

  • If the extension is unknown to the server, it MUST ignore the argument.
  • If the extension is known but not specifically permitted to be enabled with ENABLE, it MUST ignore the argument. Knowing about an extension does not necessarily mean supporting it.
  • If the extension is supported and needs to be enabled, it MUST enable it for the rest of the connection.

A server that supports ENABLE advertises the word ENABLE in its capability list. If the command succeeds, the server MUST send an untagged ENABLED response.
sections.eli5: You hand the server a list of features you want. It skips ones it has never heard of, and switches on the ones it can do. Once on, they stay on until you hang up.

sections.title: When and How Often to Use It
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD only include extensions that need to be enabled by the server. At the time of publication, CONDSTORE is the only such extension, so ENABLE CONDSTORE is an additional CONDSTORE enabling command as defined in RFC 4551. Future RFCs may add to this list.

ENABLE is only valid in the authenticated state, before any mailbox is selected. Clients MUST NOT issue it once they SELECT or EXAMINE a mailbox, although servers do not have to check this.

The command can be issued several times and is additive: ENABLE a b followed by ENABLE c equals a single ENABLE a b c. Each ENABLED response SHOULD only list the extensions enabled by its own command. There are no limits on pipelining, so a client can send ENABLE and then SELECT straight away, or a LOGIN immediately followed by ENABLE.
sections.eli5: You can ask for features more than once, and the answers add up. Just ask before you open a mailbox, not after.

sections.title: The ENABLED Response and Capability List
sections.content:
The untagged ENABLED response is the server's answer. It holds a space-separated list of the capability names that the server supports and that were successfully enabled. It may be empty, which means none of the extensions the client listed were enabled.

The server MUST NOT change the CAPABILITY list as a result of executing ENABLE. A CAPABILITY command issued right after ENABLE MUST list the same capabilities as one issued before it.

In the RFC's example, the client sends t2 ENABLE CONDSTORE X-GOOD-IDEA and the server replies with an untagged ENABLED X-GOOD-IDEA line. The server did not enable CONDSTORE there, because it did not advertise it.
sections.eli5: The server replies with the list of things it really switched on. If it switched on nothing, the list is empty.

sections.title: Advice to Extension Designers
sections.content:
The RFC discourages designers from creating extensions that require ENABLE unless there is no good alternative design. Extensions that cause potentially incompatible behavior changes to deployed server responses, and so benefit from ENABLE, have a higher complexity cost than extensions that do not.

In other words, ENABLE is a tool for the awkward cases, not the default way to add a feature.
sections.eli5: Asking for permission is a bit of a hassle, so people who invent new features should try not to need it.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is written in ABNF and builds on RFC 5234 and RFC 3501, which define the non-terminals capability and command-any. It adds ENABLE as a capability, an ENABLE command taking one or more capabilities, and an ENABLED response with zero or more capabilities.

Alphabetic characters are case-insensitive, and implementations MUST accept the strings case-insensitively.
sections.eli5: The exact grammar says what a valid ENABLE line looks like. It does not matter whether you use capital letters.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The authors believe the extension does not add any security considerations beyond those already present in base IMAP, RFC 3501.

For IANA, the document adds ENABLE to the IMAP4 Capabilities Registry.
sections.eli5: This does not open any new doors for trouble. It just gets a new name in the official list of IMAP features.
